01
Built

Original transmission schematic and isometric render from the design brief.

3D CAD assembly of the gear transmission, modeled in Autodesk Inventor.

Designed a single-stage gear transmission to transmit 14 hp over a 6,000-hour design life. Applied the Lewis bending-stress equation and DE-Goodman fatigue criteria to size gears, shafts, and bearings, then produced a full 3D assembly and dimensioned 2D manufacturing drawings in Autodesk Inventor, validated with a 3D-printed physical build.

Autodesk Inventor Lewis Bending Equation DE-Goodman Fatigue 3D Printed

Input speed had to step down from 1,500 rpm to roughly 75 rpm while carrying 14 hp, with the input and output shafts in-line and extending 4 in outside the gearbox, a center distance between 5.5–10 in, and an overall shaft length under 16 in. Gears specified in ASTM A602 M8501 steel, shafts in as-rolled 1050 steel, at a 20° pressure angle, sized for a 4,000–8,000-hour (6,000-hour design) service life under light-to-moderate, intermittent loading.

Manufacturability check: final dimensions were reviewed against a real gear manufacturer (Wire EDM Services, Simpsonville, SC) to confirm the design was actually producible, not just theoretically valid.
Power / Speed14 hp · 1,500 → 75 rpm (20:1)
Gear teethN₁=N₃=18T (pinions) · N₂=N₄=80T (gears)
Pitch diametersd₁=d₃=2.93 in · d₂=d₄=13.06 in
Center distance8 in
Diametral pitchP ≈ 6.13 → rounded to 6
Face widthb = 1.60 in (bounds: 1.47–2.28 in)
Tangential loadFₜ = 588.24 lb
Shaft diameter1.25 in nominal · 1.875 in at bearing shoulder
Bearings35 mm bore, L00-series radial ball, L07
  • Solved gear-train kinematics to fix tooth counts and pitch diameters, then applied the Lewis bending-stress equation (load, size, and velocity factors k₀, kₘ, kᵥ) to size the face width against the corrected bending-fatigue strength of the gear material.
  • Built 2D free-body diagrams of the countershaft in both the XZ and YZ planes, solved bearing reactions at A and B, and combined them into the resultant bending moment at the pinion (|M| = 1,348.32 lb·in) and transmitted torque (T = 588.24 lb·in).
  • Sized the shaft diameter with the DE-Goodman fatigue design equation, iterating stress-concentration factors for a keyway (K_t bending = 2.7, K_t torsional = 2.43), first estimate 1.13 in, converged to a standard 1.25 in diameter after the K_f correction pass.
  • Selected a 35 mm-bore radial ball bearing by required dynamic load rating, then checked the shaft shoulder and fillet radius against the bearing's minimum shoulder diameter and maximum fillet radius to confirm a proper seat.
  • Modeled all four gears, both shafts, the keyway, and housing in Autodesk Inventor; produced dimensioned 2D manufacturing drawings for each part and the full assembly.
  • Built a scaled, 3D-printed physical model of the assembled gearbox to confirm the CAD geometry actually assembled and meshed as designed.

The as-built design fixed the pinion at 18 teeth and the gear at 80 teeth to hit a 20:1 reduction. Drag either slider below to see how tooth count drives output speed and torque multiplication, using the same relations used to size this gearbox.

02
Built

Safety factor simulation across the fully assembled shaft-gear system in Autodesk Inventor.

3D free-body diagram showing applied loads on gears A and B.

Full structural analysis of a nonuniform shaft carrying two gears: 3D free-body diagrams, reaction forces, and bending/torsional/transverse stress at the critical point. Principal stresses solved analytically and via Mohr's Circle, then checked against Maximum Shear Stress and Distortion Energy failure theories. Shaft deflection modeled in MATLAB with singularity functions and validated against an Autodesk Inventor safety-factor simulation.

Mohr's Circle MSS / DET Failure Theory MATLAB FEA Validation

A 1,080 mm nonuniform shaft supported by pillow-block bearings at each end, carrying two gears, a 600 mm gear (A) 400 mm from the left support and a 300 mm gear (B) 750 mm from the left support, with an 11 kN force on gear A at 20° and a reaction-solved force on gear B at 25°.

Reaction @ bearing O494.9 N (z) · 5,082.1 N (y)
Reaction @ bearing C−10,822 N (z) · 8,315.9 N (y)
Critical sectionGear B
Resultant bending moment4,094.4 N·m
Bending normal stress, σ333.65 MPa
Torsional shear stress, τ126.35 MPa
Principal stressesσ₁ = 376.08 MPa · σ₂ = −42.44 MPa
Max in-plane shearτ_max = 209.26 MPa
Principal / shear anglesθₚ = 37.1° · θₛ = 7.9°
  • Built 2D and 3D free-body diagrams and solved static equilibrium at both bearings to establish the full external loading condition on the shaft.
  • Constructed torque, bending-moment, and transverse-shear diagrams along the full shaft length, identifying gear B as the critical section.
  • Solved bending normal and torsional shear stress at the critical point, then combined them into the xy-transverse shear state at two candidate points on the cross-section.
  • Solved principal stresses and maximum in-plane shear stress two ways: analytically and graphically via Mohr's Circle, as a cross-check between methods.
  • Modeled shaft slope and deflection with MATLAB singularity functions across the full length, then cross-checked the profile against an Autodesk Inventor FEA simulation (max Inventor deflection ≈ 54 mm near the gear span; both methods agreed on location and shape, differing in magnitude due to Inventor's full 3D geometry vs. simplified beam theory).

The design was originally specified in A36 steel. Running the failure-theory numbers caught a problem before it became a build: toggle between the original and revised material to see why.

03
Built

Type-302 stainless steel tube in cross-flow: hot water (75°C, 0.5 m/s) inside, cooling fluid sweeping across the outside.

Five-layer series thermal resistance network: internal convection → internal fouling → wall conduction → external fouling → external convection.

Determined the overall heat transfer coefficient (Uo) of a Type-302 stainless steel tube in cross-flow, comparing a water-to-air configuration against water-to-water. Built a full five-layer thermal resistance network using the Dittus–Boelter and Churchill–Bernstein correlations, hand-solved and cross-checked against a custom MATLAB script, then explored velocity, material, and fouling sensitivity with a self-built HTML/JavaScript simulation tool.

Dittus–Boelter Churchill–Bernstein Thermal Resistance Network MATLAB & JS Simulation

A Type-302 stainless steel tube (22 mm ID · 27 mm OD) carries 75°C water at 0.5 m/s while a cooler fluid sweeps across the outside in cross-flow. Two external cases are investigated: air at 20 m/s and, separately, water at 1 m/s — both at 15°C. Internal and external fouling factors (0.0004 and 0.0002 m²·K/W) are included on both surfaces. Goal: find the overall heat transfer coefficient Uo for each case and identify which resistance layer actually limits performance.

Tube materialType-302 Stainless Steel, k = 15.1 W/m·K
Inner / outer diameterDⁱ = 22 mm · Dₒ = 27 mm
Internal fluidWater · 75°C · 0.5 m/s
External fluid, Case AAir · 15°C · 20 m/s
External fluid, Case BWater · 15°C · 1 m/s
Fouling factorsR''f,i = 0.0004 · R''f,o = 0.0002 m²·K/W
Correlations usedDittus–Boelter (internal) · Churchill–Bernstein (external)

Swapping the external fluid from air to water restructures the entire resistance network rather than just scaling it — the thermal bottleneck moves from one side of the tube to the other.

Uo, water-to-air94.61 W/m²·K
Uo, water-to-water686.81 W/m²·K · 7.3× higher
ho, air vs. water107.3 → 4,773.8 W/m²·K · 44.5×
Bottleneck, water-to-airExternal convection · 88.2% of total resistance
Bottleneck, water-to-waterInternal fouling · 33.7% (load spread across 4 terms)
Copper wall swap, water-to-air94.61 → 96.22 W/m²·K · +1.7% (not worth it)
Copper wall swap, water-to-water686.81 → 781.42 W/m²·K · +13.8% (worth it)
Engineering takeaway: in the water-to-air case, the internal side is already so efficient that upgrading the tube material or the water-side velocity is close to wasted effort — nearly 9 out of every 10 units of resistance sit on the air side. Once the external fluid is water, no single term dominates, so the more effective lever shifts to fouling control and, only then, wall material.
  • Built the governing thermal-resistance-network model (Rtot = Rcv,i + Rf,i + Rw + Rf,o + Rcv,o) from first-principles conduction and convection equations, referenced to the tube's outer surface area.
  • Interpolated fluid properties (ρ, μ, k, Pr) from standard tables at each stream's film temperature, then solved internal Reynolds/Nusselt/h using Dittus–Boelter and external Reynolds/Nusselt/h using Churchill–Bernstein for both the air and water cross-flow cases.
  • Tabulated all five resistances and their percent contribution to the total for each case, then compared side-by-side to identify how the dominant term shifts with fluid choice.
  • Cross-checked every hand-solved result against a MATLAB script performing the same single-point and parametric calculations.
  • Wrote a standalone HTML/JavaScript simulation tool (embedded live below) to sweep internal and external velocity, material, and fouling factors, and generated the parametric and sensitivity figures used throughout the write-up from its output.
  • Evaluated a tube-material swap to copper for both configurations and ran a fouling-doubling sensitivity case to quantify long-term performance risk.

This is the actual simulation tool built for the project — live, not a screenshot. Switch the external fluid, drag the velocity and fouling sliders, or swap the tube material, and every readout, resistance bar, and the velocity-sweep curve recompute in real time from the same equations used in the hand calculations above.
